rendering.native: 800 × 450 SVG painted by Resvg on the real 30 fps scene clock.
rendering.browser: Pinned chromium-headless-shell revision 1248, Chromium 156.0.8078.4, DPR 1. Each primary case has lossless native browser frames and a paired 30 fps MP4 encoded from full native Resvg captures.
rendering.phone: 358 × 201.375 CSS-pixel whole picture in a 358 × 202 pixel screenshot, DPR 1. The image pairs place the two real phone screenshots side by side.
rendering.clock: Event-relative f0 is the picture before the first transition frame. Reader captures also include an explicit last draw. A held shorter video side is labeled. Only the pre-event picture exists for a guard.
rendering.interpretation: The reviewer examined paired temporal contact sequences, the native images and selected target-specific knockout controls. Causality, movement and pacing use the progression across the event and the authored caption. Exact byte and pixel comparisons support claims of identical output.
rendering.scale: Phone glyph heights use the change in the browser screenshot after removing the exact moving text outlines, with an eight-level RGB threshold. They do not predict every reader’s visual acuity.

authoredStep.title: The agent seals what it sends
authoredStep.line: The seal says which agent is asking, and for which User.
authoredStep.caption: The agent adds a medium to the cart. The request carries a Session header, drawn as the wax seal, signed with the agent’s published keys. The Company now knows the agent, a User ID and a Session for the cart. The User ID is a pseudonym made for this Company, so the shop still does not know you. Your agent signs every request to say who is asking, and you approve separately what it may do with your account.

authoredStep.title: You hand over a key, not your password
authoredStep.line: Standard OAuth, on the Company’s own page.
authoredStep.caption: The agent sends you to the Company’s sign-in page. You sign in there and approve orders:read and orders:write. The Company gives the agent an access token, drawn as a key with one tooth for each scope you approved. Your password stays with you, and the Company can take this one key back without locking you out. Sign-in does not mention the Session: what the Company knows has not changed.

authoredStep.title: When the seal itself is wrong
authoredStep.line: 400 invalid_session: fix the cause. A new Session won’t.
authoredStep.caption: Now the number changes. The delegation that vouches for the agent’s signing key has expired, and the slip says 400 invalid_session, about the seal. authoredStep.title: The slip says what to bring
authoredStep.line: invalid_token: refresh the key, send it again.
authoredStep.caption: The agent trades its refresh token for a new access token, without asking you, and sends the same request: 200, the exchange is made. Each refusal’s code names its own remedy, and the agent applies that one: the wrong one loops, or throws away a good token. Had you disconnected the agent from your account, the refresh would fail, and the agent would carry on signed out.

authoredStep.title: Punched in order
authoredStep.line: All 11 checks hold, two of them optional.
authoredStep.caption: The shop walks the chain from iss down to the seal, then the claims: typed as a Session JWT, addressed to this shop, for this method and URL, signed a second ago, covering the token it carries. authoredStep.title: The wrong hand on the seal
authoredStep.line: Another agent’s seal, or the published key: refused.

authoredStep.title: The agent opens the Company’s own page
authoredStep.line: It asks for two scopes, and nothing more.
authoredStep.caption: Poppy’s way is OAuth. The agent opens example.com’s sign-in page in your browser and asks for the two scopes the exchange needs, orders:read and orders:write, and not addresses. The Company describes each scope and warns that orders:write can’t be undone. The request carries a fingerprint of the agent’s secret PKCE verifier, so only the agent can finish this sign-in, and prompt=consent, so the page appears even for scopes you approved before: a forwarded link cannot get tokens without it.

authoredStep.title: A handshake with the issuer
authoredStep.line: The domain names its issuer; the issuer names it back.
authoredStep.caption: Who issues this shop’s tokens? example.com’s protected resource metadata, the signpost, names auth.example.com. The agent then asks the issuer, whose own metadata lists example.com among its domains. Each side points at the other, and from now on the Company is known by its issuer. That is the answer: The domain names its issuer and the issuer lists the domain back, and each check stops one way to impersonate the shop. Three forgers now try to get round one check each.

cases.intendedClaim: The fetched sheet dropped from the address bar straight down over the shop’s fascia to the doorstep, while the address was still changing; the fix changes the address first and brings a document down the street beside the shop.

The claimed fascia crossing is absent on this route.

authoredStep.title: The file speaks for the host that served it
authoredStep.line: It must name that host itself.
authoredStep.caption: The agent fetches www.example.com/.well-known/poppy.json over HTTPS, and the shop redirects it to the same path on example.com, which is allowed. The file lists the ways in, at least one of them: the shop’s APIs, its website and its own agent, beside sign-in details, tasks and extensions. Its letterhead, organization.domain, says example.com, and the agent checks that this is the host that served it.
